boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's action (Gefecht) at Saalfeld on 10 October 1806 in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: Prince Louis Ferdinand's decision on the evening of the 9th, his advance from Rudolstadt to Saalfeld, the attack of Marshal Lannes's corps, the prince's death and the rout across the Saale and the Schwarza, with General Pelet's detachment at Blankenburg, and the losses. Napoleon's orders for the 10th and the advance of the French centre by Schleiz are context; Jena (B372a) and Auerstedt (B373a) are separate entries. Side A is the French. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 12,000 men with 14 guns under Marshal Lannes, and side B (Prussians and Saxons) 8 battalions and 7 squadrons, 9,000 men with 42 guns, under Lieutenant-General Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia, whose name he marks with a dagger (claim bodart-commanders). By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His 12,000 for side A lies between the French reports of the troops engaged, Lannes's hardly more than 4,000 of the division Suchet and the 2nd Bulletin's half of that division (claim foucart-side-a), and Höpfner's estimate of about 14,000 French engaged (claim hoepfner-side-a); no return of Lannes's corps was found (open questions). His 14 guns equal General Foucher's 2 four-pounders that fired from the start and the 10 eight-pounders and 2 howitzers that arrived at the end of the action (our arithmetic; claim foucart-side-a). His 9,000 for side B is above Höpfner's 8300 for the prince's advanced guard and the 8000 available in Höpfner's first reason for the defeat (claim hoepfner-side-b); his 7 squadrons are fewer than Höpfner's 9 in second line and the one left with the light troops, 10 in all (our arithmetic); his 42 guns are more than the 27 pieces whose fire Foucher's 2 four-pounders sustained (claim foucart-side-b) and the 33 guns lost in Höpfner's account (claim side-b-losses-reported). The figures are forces available, which the commanders' dispositions shaped, so the phase is unresolved. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the French (12,000 men with 14 guns) under Marshal Lannes over the Prussians and Saxons (8 battalions, 7 squadrons = 9,000 men with 42 guns) under Lieutenant-General Prince Louis Ferdinand of Prussia †'. 'Gen.-Lt.' is General-Leutnant, 'Pz.' Prinz, 'Btln.' Bataillon and 'Esk.' Eskadron in Bodart's list of abbreviations.

claims.value: Side A (French) in the documents Foucart prints: Marshal Lannes wrote to the Emperor from Saalfeld at 7 in the evening of 10 October 1806 that he had set out that morning at 5 with his army corps, that hardly more than 4,000 men of the division Suchet had been engaged and the division Gazan was still 2 leagues from him, and that the 9th and 10th hussars had made a fine charge; the 2nd Bulletin, dated at Auma on 12 October 1806, says that half of General Suchet's division alone was engaged and that the 9th and 10th hussar regiments overthrew the Prussian cavalry. General Foucher, commanding the 5th corps's artillery, reported on 11 October 1806 that the division Suchet's park had been caught in the gorges, so that only 2 four-pounders attached to the advanced-guard brigade fired from the start of the action to its end, and that 10 eight-pounders and 2 howitzers arrived at its end. General Suchet's report names the 34th and the 17th, the 64th and detached companies of the 34th, and the elite battalion among the troops that took the enemy's guns. Marshal Augereau, receiving Lannes's letter later that day, could not come to his help as quickly as he wished, his last orders sending him to Coburg, but set his corps in march to join him at Saalfeld (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 464, 465, 474, 497, 522 and 524) except Augereau's letter and the heading of Suchet's report (OCR). The French documents count only the troops that fought: Lannes's 4,000 and the Bulletin's half of the division Suchet leave out the cavalry and the division Gazan, and Foucher's report has most of the guns that fired arrive only at the end; Bodart's 12,000 (claim bodart-strength) and Höpfner's about 14,000 (claim hoepfner-side-a) are larger. Bodart's 14 guns equal Foucher's 2 four-pounders, 10 eight-pounders and 2 howitzers (our arithmetic). No return of Lannes's corps was found in the volume (open questions). Which troops and guns fought followed from the timing of Lannes's attack and from the gorges (claims side-a-command and saalfeld-ground), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Saalfeld, 10 October 1806, 7 o'clock in the evening'; 'I set out this morning at 5 o'clock with my army corps to go to Saalfeld, where I found the corps commanded by Prince Louis of Prussia, who was killed by a hussar of the 10th regiment' (p. 464); 'hardly more than 4,000 men of the division Suchet were engaged'; 'the division Gazan was still 2 leagues from me'; 'I must not leave Your Majesty unaware of the fine charge that the 9th and 10th hussars made' (p. 465); the Bulletin, '2nd Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Auma, 12 October 1806' (p. 522); 'the cannonade lasted only two hours; half of General Suchet's division alone was engaged; the Prussian cavalry was overthrown by the 9th and 10th hussar regiments' (p. 524); Foucher, 'General Foucher, commanding the artillery of the 5th corps, to General Songis'; 'Saalfeld, 11 October 1806'; 'the artillery of the 5th corps made up yesterday, by the skill of the gunners and their bravery, for the small number of pieces that circumstances allowed to be put in battery: the park of the division Suchet having been caught in the gorges, 2 four-pounders alone, attached to the advanced-guard brigade, were able to fire from the beginning and take part in the action to its end; these 2 pieces alone sustained the fire of 27 pieces'; 'there were consumed 264 rounds of 4; 10 eight-pounders and 2 howitzers that arrived at the end of the action fired 63 rounds in all' (p. 497); Suchet, 'report of General Suchet on the combat of Saalfeld' (OCR); 'a good number of prisoners (1,500 or 1,800) and 17 pieces of cannon were carried off by the 34th and the 17th in the wood on the left, where the enemy had crowded them'; 'two others were [taken] by the 64th and the detached companies of the 34th'; 'another piece was taken by the elite battalion at Rudolstadt, where it must have stayed' (p. 474); Augereau, 'Marshal Augereau to Marshal Lannes at Saalfeld'; 'my dear Marshal, it is ... o'clock in the evening and I receive your letter dated from Saalfeld, by which you inform me that you are before that town, occupied by the enemy, which you are going to have attacked at once'; 'I am in despair, my dear Marshal, at not being able to fly to your help as promptly as I would wish; but the last orders I have received from Prince Alexandre order me to go to Coburg without giving me any instructions'; 'nevertheless I order the ... army corps to set out to join you at Saalfeld' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A in Höpfner: of the French only the advanced guard, the division Suchet and the cavalry of Lannes's corps fought, so that about 14,000 men went into action against 8,300, if the troops at Blankenburg and the 2nd battalion Müffling at Schwarza are counted; the division Gazan reached the field only later. While the brigade Wedell marched off to the left, the brigade Claparède (the 34th and 40th of the line and the 17th light infantry) and the corps's cavalry remained under cover.
claims.rationale: Höpfner's estimate, read from the page images (pp. 275 and 284); the passages read give no source for it. His 14,000 is above Bodart's 12,000 (claim bodart-strength) and far above Lannes's own hardly more than 4,000 of the division Suchet engaged and the 2nd Bulletin's half of that division (claim foucart-side-a), which leave out the cavalry and the advanced guard that Höpfner counts. Which French troops fought followed the timing of Lannes's attack (claim side-a-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'of the French only the advanced guard, the division Suchet and the cavalry of Lannes's corps had fought, so that about 14,000 men had gone into action against 8,300 men, if one wishes to count in the troops at Blankenburg and the 2nd battalion Müffling at Schwarza'; 'the division Gazan arrived on the battlefield only later' (p. 284); 'he no doubt soon recognised that there was no question of any significant attack, and therefore did not let himself be disturbed in his march to the left with the brigade Wedell, while the brigade Claparède — 34th and 40th line and 17th light infantry regiments — and the corps's cavalry remained halted under cover, and only the skirmishers at the foot of the heights were considerably reinforced' (p. 275).

claims.value: Side B in the documents Foucart prints: Lannes wrote that the corps under the prince's orders appeared to have been made up of 5 regiments, 3 Saxon and 2 Prussian, and 4 regiments of hussars, 2 Saxon and 2 Prussian; General Foucher reported that the 2 French four-pounders in action from the start sustained alone the fire of 27 pieces. M. de Mumpfling, an engineer in the King of Saxony's service, in a report Foucart prints in a note in French translation, gives Prince Hohenlohe's advanced guard, formed in cantonments between Arnstadt and Saalfeld on 7 October 1806 under the Prussian generals Schimmelpfenning and Pellet and the Saxon generals Trutzschlen and Bevilaqua, as 18 squadrons of cavalry, 9 battalions and 2 companies of infantry and 3 batteries, joined by 2 Saxon battalions of Prince Xavier; on 9 October the prince concentrated the corps near Rudolstadt but left the outposts on the heights from Oberhof to Kahlert, Major-General Schimmelpfenning with his 5 squadrons at Oppurg, and Major-General Pellet with 3 battalions of Prussian fusiliers, 1 company of foot chasseurs, half a battery of light artillery and 3 squadrons of Saxon hussars at Blankenburg.
claims.rationale: Lannes's letter, Mumpfling's report (p. 464) and Foucher's report (p. 497), read from the page images. Mumpfling's composition is of the whole advanced guard before its concentration, including the detachments at Oppurg and Blankenburg, so it is not the force at Saalfeld; Höpfner's 8300 for the advanced guard (claim hoepfner-side-b) and Bodart's 9,000 (claim bodart-strength) are the closest figures. Lannes's regiments are a description from the field, not a count, and Foucher's 27 pieces are the guns that fired on the French, fewer than Bodart's 42. Which troops fought followed the prince's dispositions (claim prince-decision), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Lannes, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading and date; 'it appears that the corps under his orders was composed of 5 regiments, of which 3 Saxon and 2 Prussian, and of 4 regiments of hussars, of which 2 Saxon and 2 Prussian'; Mumpfling, 'report made by M. de Mumpfling, engineer in the service of H. M. the King of Saxony, on the affair of Saalfeld'; '(this translation is in the archives of the War [ministry])'; 'on 7 October 1806 Prince Hohenlohe's advanced guard formed in cantonments between Arnstadt and Saalfeld under the Prussian generals Schimmelpfenning and Pellet and the Saxon [generals] Trutzschlen and Bevilaqua. It was composed of 18 squadrons of cavalry, 9 battalions and 2 companies of infantry, 3 batteries, to which were joined 2 Saxon battalions of Prince Xavier'; 'on 9 October the prince concentrated the corps near Rudolstadt, but he left the outposts on the heights from Oberhof to Kahlert, Major-General Schimmelpfenning with his 5 squadrons at Oppurg, and Major-General Pellet with 3 battalions of Prussian fusiliers, 1 company of foot chasseurs, half a battery of light artillery and 3 squadrons of Saxon hussars at Blankenburg'; 'he strengthened the advanced guard with the 2 Saxon battalions of Prince Xavier' (p. 464); Foucher, as in claim foucart-side-a (p. 497).

claims.value: Side B in Höpfner: on the night of the 9th to the 10th the advanced guard under Prince Louis, 8300 men in all, gathered gradually in the evening and the night, and General Schimmelpfennig stood with 5 squadrons, 600 men, at Oppurg between Pösneck and Neustadt. At Saalfeld Colonel Rabenau had the other 3 companies of his fusilier battalion between the town and the Rabenstein, with the 12 guns of the 6-pounder battery Riemann, which had marched to Saalfeld by a misunderstanding instead of to the prince's rendezvous, and the half horse battery Gause on his right, and the 3 squadrons of Schimmelpfennig hussars further right and forward. The prince left a company of the Saxon regiment Xaver at the Saale bridge before Rudolstadt, assembled the main body of the advanced guard at 7 between Rudolstadt and Volkstädt and marched without waiting for the regiment Müffling. For his last advance the regiments Kurfürst and Xaver, 3½ weak battalions, went forward, while all the cavalry but one squadron left with the jäger and fusiliers, 9 squadrons, covered them in second line. Höpfner counts 8,300 men against the French if the troops at Blankenburg and the 2nd battalion Müffling at Schwarza are included, and judges that the prince spread the 8000 men available over 1 Meile, from Saalfeld to Blankenburg.
claims.rationale: Höpfner's figures, read from the page images (pp. 255, 268, 275 and 284). His 8300 is the advanced guard as assembled for the 10th, below Bodart's 9,000 (claim bodart-strength), and his 8000 the force available in his first reason for the defeat (claim side-b-objectives). The 9 squadrons of the last advance and the one left with the light troops make 10 (our arithmetic), against Bodart's 7; the battalions were 3½ because a company of the regiment Xaver had stayed at Rudolstadt. Which troops fought followed the prince's dispositions: he marched without waiting for the regiment Müffling and left General Pelet at Blankenburg (claim prince-decision), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'Hohenlohe's corps stood as follows in the night from the 9th to the 10th'; 'General Schimmelpfennig with 5 squadrons, 600 men, at Oppurg between Pösneck and Neustadt'; 'the advanced guard under Prince Louis, together 8300 men, which gathered gradually in the evening and in the night, so that at the departure only the hussar posts in the Thuringian Forest at Oberhof and Kahlert, and a detachment' [the sentence continues] (p. 255); 'Colonel Rabenau had placed, as it were in a 2nd line behind Captain Gneisenau's detachment but separated from it by a hollow and gardens, the remaining 3 companies of his fusilier battalion between the town and the Rabenstein, the left wing at the town; on the right wing the 12 guns of the 6-pounder battery Riemann — which by a misunderstanding had marched not to the rendezvous the prince had named but to Saalfeld — and the ½ horse battery Gause on a gentle rise'; 'the 3 squadrons of Schimmelpfennig hussars further to the right and forward, in troops, toward the exits of the mountains'; 'the prince, after leaving a company of the Saxon regiment Xaver, which had joined him, at the Saale bridge before Rudolstadt, had assembled the main body of the advanced guard at 7 o'clock in a column marched off by the right between Rudolstadt and Volkstädt, and set it in march without waiting for the regiment Müffling, which was to have the head but had stood furthest off, as far as Remda' (p. 268); 'as soon as the battalions named above were in motion, the prince had the regiment Kurfürst align again with the regiment Xaver and these 3½ weak battalions advance in battalion echelons from the right wing, with music playing, against the height from which the high road comes down'; '1 company of the regiment Xaver had stayed behind at Rudolstadt'; 'all the cavalry — except one squadron, which remained with the jäger and fusiliers — that is 9 squadrons, received the order to cover the attacking battalions in second line and with wide intervals between Wölsdorf and Saalfeld' (p. 275); 'the endeavour of Prince Louis to hold at the same time the point of Saalfeld and the retreat on Rudolstadt; two aims which he believed he could reach only by the undue extension of the available 8000 men over the stretch of 1 Meile, or from Saalfeld to Blankenburg, with the Saale at his back'; and as in claim hoepfner-side-a for the 8,300 (p. 284).

claims.value: Side A's command: at 5 in the morning of 10 October 1806 Napoleon wrote to the grand-duc de Berg that Marshal Lannes had arrived at Gräfenthal on the evening of the 9th and would attack Saalfeld 'tomorrow', and that he wanted to know of the movement on Saalfeld during the day so that, if the enemy had gathered more than 25,000 men there, he could send reinforcements by Pösneck and take them in the rear. At 6 the major general wrote to Lannes that the Emperor approved his dispositions: he was to hasten the arrival of Marshal Augereau and immediately afterwards attack Saalfeld. In Höpfner, Lannes had received from Napoleon, from Nordhalben, the repeated order for the 10th to undertake nothing before joining Augereau if the Prussians meant to defend Saalfeld seriously, to take position at Gräfenthal if they concentrated all their forces there, and, if they were only some 15—18,000 strong, to reconnoitre their position and attack them, but together with Augereau, and to seize Saalfeld quickly if they retreated (the last clause OCR); an order from Ebersdorf that morning told Augereau to join Lannes by forced marches, Lannes having orders to attack Saalfeld in concert with him (OCR). Lannes attacked before Augereau or his own division Gazan came up: he wrote that he had set out at 5 that morning, that brisk firing heard toward the centre corps, where the Emperor was, had led him to attack, thinking his movement would make a diversion in favour of the centre, and that the division Gazan was still 2 leagues away. Augereau, receiving his letter later that day, regretted that Lannes had not told him of his movements before leaving, as he could have made his operations coincide (OCR). On the field, in General Suchet's report and the corps journal's extracts in it (OCR), Lannes ordered Suchet to have the crests of the heights over the gorge of Saalfeld taken, ordered the cavalry and the division Suchet forward once convinced that the enemy meant to fight, and seized the moment to order the charge, and a note to the report has him at the head of the infantry; in Höpfner he reconnoitred the Prussian position and the ground, had Suchet debouch with the corps's advanced guard from the valley of Garnsdorf while the corps's cavalry and the division moved along the ridge toward Blankenburg to take from the prince his retreat on Rudolstadt, and had the fight in front pressed to hold the prince before the town while the turning movement took effect (OCR). Höpfner calls the manœuvre skilful but prescribed by circumstances (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 456, 457, 262, 464 and 465), with the order to Augereau, Augereau's letter, Suchet's report and the rest of Höpfner's narrative from the OCR. Napoleon's orders provided for an attack on Saalfeld together with Augereau; Lannes attacked alone, before Augereau or his division Gazan came up, on hearing the firing toward the centre, so the decision to fight when he did was his own and the claim is tagged commander_created. Napoleon's letter, dated 5 in the morning of the 10th, says that Lannes 'will attack Saalfeld tomorrow'; the passages read do not explain the word. Höpfner gives no source for the Nordhalben order in the passages read. English renderings (ours): 'the Emperor to the grand-duc de Berg, at Schleiz'; 'imperial headquarters of Ebersdorf, 10 October 1806, 5 o'clock in the morning'; 'Marshal Lannes arrived at Gräfenthal on the evening of the 9th; he will attack Saalfeld tomorrow'; 'you know how important it is for me to know during the day of the movement on Saalfeld, so that, if the enemy had gathered more than 25,000 men there, I could march reinforcements there by Pösneck and take them in the rear' (p. 456); 'the major general to Marshal Lannes'; 'Ebersdorf, 10 October 1806, 6 o'clock in the morning'; 'the Emperor, Monsieur le Maréchal, approves the dispositions you have made; hasten the arrival of Marshal Augereau and immediately afterwards attack Saalfeld' (p. 457); 'on the left wing Marshal Lannes had pushed back Prince Louis's advanced cavalry detachments, had advanced with the 5th corps as far as Gräfenthal and had received from Napoleon, from Nordhalben, the repeated order for the 10th:'; '„that, if the Prussians wished to defend Saalfeld seriously, he should undertake nothing before the junction with Marshal Augereau — that, if the opponent concentrated all his forces at Saalfeld, he had nothing to do but take position at Gräfenthal — that the Prussians could not dare to attack him, since they had such considerable forces on their left flank, but that if they nevertheless dared, he could indeed begin the retreat, since they would then be attacked in the flank by the column of the centre — that if, however, the opponent were only some 15—18,000 men strong, he should reconnoitre his position well and attack him, but in union with Marshal Augereau — that it was important to send him — Napoleon — reports three times a day — that, if the Prussians' (p. 262); '[began the] retreat, he should quickly seize Saalfeld and post himself there militarily.”' (OCR); 'Ebersdorf, ... claims.value: Side B's command: Prince Hohenlohe's order, sent to Prince Louis at Stadt-Ilm by Captain Valentini during the night, was to defend the posts of Rudolstadt and Blankenburg with the advanced guard, to be assembled at Rudolstadt, until the main army's advanced guard arrived, and then to withdraw across the Saale toward Rahnis and Pösneck, where with General Count Tauentzien he was to form the advanced guard of the left-wing army gathering at Mittel-Pöllnitz (OCR); M. de Mumpfling gives it as an express order to keep the posts of Blankenburg and Rudolstadt until Lieutenant-General Blücher, commanding the King's advanced guard, arrived, to hand them over to him and then to withdraw to Pösneck. The prince sent Lieutenant Count Caraman of the artillery to the Duke of Brunswick at Blankenhayn and Lieutenant Wagner of the Saxon hussars to Hohenlohe; what Wagner was charged to tell Hohenlohe could not be established (OCR). Hohenlohe's answer, brought back by Lieutenant Egidi, was given not to the prince but to his adjutant, Lieutenant Nostitz: the prince was to stay in the position he had taken and not attack; Hohenlohe added that he himself had orders to hold the lines covered by the Saale valley (OCR). Höpfner holds it certain that neither Egidi nor any adjutant told the prince of the forbidden crossing of the Saale; in Mumpfling's report the Saxon lieutenant brought the prince himself a verbal order from Hohenlohe to stay in the position of Rudolstadt and not attack (OCR). Under the prince, General Trützschler commanded the cavalry before the town, General Bevilaqua with the regiment Klemens followed a battalion of the regiment Müffling to occupy the wooded height called the obere Hayn, and an officer was sent to General Pelet at Blankenburg to keep the defile of the Schwarza occupied and cover the prince's right flank (OCR); in Mumpfling's report Pelet, first ordered by the prince to advance on Saalfeld, was countermanded and went back to Blankenburg to hold the crossing of the Schwarza and to seek to make a diversion on Lannes's left flank (OCR).
claims.rationale: Höpfner's account of the orders and messages from the OCR, with Mumpfling's version of Hohenlohe's order from the page image (p. 464) and the rest of his report from the OCR. Hohenlohe's order was to hold Rudolstadt and Blankenburg and then cross the Saale; his answer reached the prince's adjutant, not the prince, and by Höpfner's account nobody told the prince of the forbidden crossing, while in Mumpfling's report the order reached the prince. The prince's advance to Saalfeld and his fight there were his own decision, beyond his orders (claim prince-decision), so the claim is tagged commander_created. claims.value: Prince Louis's decision: riding from Stadt-Ilm to Rudolstadt he received Colonel Rabenau's report from Saalfeld that the enemy, 16—20,000 strong, was advancing from Coburg on Gräfenthal and would to all appearances attack Saalfeld seriously the next day, but he doubted that very considerable forces would come by the Saale valley. Knowing only that he was to march across the Saale to Pösneck on the 10th while Hohenlohe's main body debouched at Orlamünde, Kahla and Jena, and having learned that no usable road led from Rudolstadt to Pösneck but the carriage road through Saalfeld, he judged that if the enemy took Saalfeld his advanced guard would be barred from the crossing and cut off from the corps, and the enemy could use the bridge at Saalfeld and the good road to Neustadt to fall on the flank of the corps and reach Neustadt first (the last part OCR). That consideration, the magazine at Saalfeld and his view that General Pelet at Blankenburg and General Schimmelpfennig at Pösneck covered his flanks made it important to him not to let Saalfeld be taken by a false attack, a mere demonstration (OCR). He wrote to the King asking that part of the main army be thrown into the Saale valley and advanced on Gräfenthal, sent a copy to Hohenlohe, and, to keep the bridge at Saalfeld for his own crossing until the main army's troops could arrive, thought it necessary to advance against the town himself and hold it for a time; he told Colonel Rabenau that he would support him seriously, ordered the advanced guard to the rendezvous between Schwarza and Rudolstadt at daybreak, and informed Pelet and Schimmelpfennig, who were to stay at Blankenburg and Pösneck (OCR). He was in high spirits at the prospect of beating off an attack on Saalfeld and then, after crossing the Saale, throwing himself against the enemy advancing by Schleiz. He assembled the main body of the advanced guard at 7 and set it in march without waiting for the regiment Müffling, and took up a position that Höpfner calls not especially advantageous for defence, believing he could await the enemy's movements there (OCR). When the enemy's evident superiority was put to him he made no reply and rode forward to reconnoitre; probably recognising that he must retreat, but still believing in Hohenlohe's crossing of the Saale, he resolved on a last attempt to hold up the enemy by making a show of attacking; at the end he put himself at the head of the Saxon squadrons that threw themselves on the French flank, and was killed when he answered the call to surrender with his sword (OCR). The 2nd Bulletin has him fight hand to hand with a quartermaster-sergeant of the 10th hussars, answer the call to surrender with a sabre stroke and fall to a thrust. In Mumpfling's report the prince, no doubt little informed of the strength of the French corps, resolved to forestall the attack and give battle to save Saalfeld, where there was a magazine; he had resolved to attack the enemy if it advanced, held back not even by Hohenlohe's order, believed himself sure of victory, and, seeing his infantry in disorder, led the cavalry himself in an attack (OCR). Clausewitz, as Höpfner quotes him, wrote that he overrated the effect of his courage and wanted the impossible (OCR).
claims.rationale: The prince's reasoning and orders in Höpfner, partly from the page images (pp. 260, 262 and 268) and partly from the OCR; the Bulletin from the page images (pp. 522 and 524); Mumpfling's report from the page image (p. 464) and the OCR. The accounts agree that the decision to advance from Rudolstadt to Saalfeld and to fight there was the prince's own, beyond Hohenlohe's order to hold Rudolstadt and Blankenburg (claim side-b-command), so the claim is tagged commander_created; they differ on his intent, Höpfner's prince defending the crossing and then making a show of attack, Mumpfling's resolved on battle (claim posture). The list of misprints in Höpfner's front matter corrects the passage on the bridge. 'the prince, however, doubted that very considerable forces would advance in the Saale valley, but rather believed that the enemy would direct his main forces by Schleiz against the left flank of the Prussian army on the right bank of the Saale'; 'since he knew no other than that he was to march across the Saale to Pösneck on the 10th, and that the main body of Hohenlohe's corps would at the same time debouch at Orlamünde, Kahla and Jena toward Mittel-Pöllnitz, but by the inquiries made no usable road led from Rudolstadt to Pösneck, the carriage road going instead by Saalfeld, it seemed to him that if the enemy seized the point of Saalfeld, not only would his own advanced guard be denied the crossing of the Saale and thereby from the main body of the corps' (p. 260); 'could be cut off, but the enemy would also be put in a position to use the bridge at Saalfeld, to march on the good road to Neustadt, to fall on the flank of the corps defiling on bad mountain roads, and to reach Neustadt before it'; 'this consideration, the presence of a magazine in Saalfeld, as well as the view that his right flank was sufficiently covered by General Pelet's position at Blankenburg and his left flank by General Schimmelpfennig at Pösneck, made it important to the prince not to let the point of Saalfeld be taken by a false attack, by a mere demonstration'; claims.value: Bodart codes the action (Gefecht) at Saalfeld on 10 October 1806 as a victory of the French under Marshal Lannes over the Prussians and Saxons under Prince Louis Ferdinand. claims.value: Side B's losses as reported: Lannes wrote on the evening of the action that about 800 prisoners had been taken, many men killed or drowned and 21 guns taken, that he expected 6 more to be gathered with about 20 caissons and at least 3 colours, and that among the prisoners were a Prussian general, 3 or 4 colonels, as many lieutenant-colonels and about 30 officers; on the next morning he wrote that he had told the Emperor he would have the artillery, 36 to 40 pieces, taken to Kronach, and that many more dead and drowned had been left on the field than had been thought (the latter OCR). General Suchet's report has a good number of prisoners, 1,500 or 1,800 in a parenthesis, and 17 guns taken by the 34th and the 17th in the wood on the left, two more by the 64th and detached companies of the 34th and another by the elite battalion at Rudolstadt, and, in another parenthesis, 1,500 or 1,800 prisoners, 4 colours and 33 guns with their caissons. General Foucher's artillery report gives 25 guns, 2 howitzers, 6 caissons and 70 draught horses as the fruit of the action; the 2nd Bulletin, 1,000 prisoners, 600 men left on the field and 30 guns, and 2 of the prince's aides-de-camp killed at his side. Höpfner gives the Prussian and Saxon loss as 5 officers killed or dead of wounds, 24 officers wounded, 17—1800 men killed, wounded and prisoners, 15 Prussian and 18 Saxon guns with their ammunition wagons, almost all the troops' baggage and 4 colours, a loss of not quite 2000 men that was painful but in no way decisive for the war; Valentini's jäger company, fighting on the extreme left from 10 in the morning to 4 in the afternoon, had only 1 officer and 3 men wounded and 4 missing. General Bevilaqua was taken (Höpfner and Mumpfling, OCR); General Trützschler and Colonels Kaphengst and Pflugk were badly wounded and Colonels Rühle and Rabenau taken (Höpfner, OCR), Mumpfling having Pflugk wounded and taken (OCR); a considerable part of the magazine at Saalfeld, chiefly forage, was saved (OCR). The prince was killed.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 464, 465, 474, 494, 497, 522, 524, 284 and 286), with the officers' fates, the dead and the magazine from the OCR. The figures differ: Lannes's about 800 prisoners on the evening of the action against the Bulletin's 1,000, the 1,500 or 1,800 in the parentheses of Suchet's report and Bodart's 1,100 (claim bodart-losses); for the guns, Lannes's 21 taken and 6 expected, 27 (our arithmetic), and his 36 to 40 of the next morning, Foucher's 25 guns and 2 howitzers, 27 (our arithmetic), the Bulletin's 30, and the 33 of the parenthesis in Suchet's report (by Foucart's note the edition puts its extracts of the corps journal in parentheses, so the parenthesized figures may be the journal's), of Höpfner's 15 Prussian and 18 Saxon (our arithmetic) and of Bodart; Suchet's 17 guns in the wood, two more and one at Rudolstadt make 20 (our arithmetic). Lannes's 'Prussian general' among the prisoners may be the Saxon General Bevilaqua, whom Höpfner and Mumpfling have taken; the passages read do not say. Höpfner's footnote on the officers killed (p. 284) was not transcribed (open questions). English renderings (ours): Lannes, 'as I think Your Majesty must be very anxious, I will content myself with telling you in two words that we have thrown the enemy into the river, taken about 800 prisoners, killed or drowned many men, [and] taken 21 pieces of cannon which are gathered at this moment'; 'I presume that 6 more will be picked up, about 20 caissons and at least 3 colours'; 'among the prisoners are a Prussian general, 3 or 4 colonels, as many lieutenant-colonels and about 30 officers' (p. 465); 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Saalfeld, 11 October 1806, 9 o'clock in the morning'; 'I had the honour of informing Your Majesty yesterday of the affair of Saalfeld. I told you that I would have the artillery, numbering 36 to 40 pieces, taken to Kronach' (p. 494); 'there remained on the battlefield many more dead and drowned than had been believed' (OCR); Suchet, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading (OCR) and the guns (p. 474); 'the road was full of abandoned baggage and caissons (1,500 or 1,800 prisoners, 4 colours, and 33 pieces of cannon with their caissons harnessed)' (p. 474); Foucher, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading and date; '25 pieces of cannon, 2 howitzers, 6 caissons, 70 draught horses are, as regards the artillery, the fruit of the affair of Saalfeld' (p. 497); the Bulletin, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading and date (p. 522); '1,000 prisoners were taken; 600 men remained on the battlefield; 30 pieces of cannon fell into the army's power'; 'two of his aides-de-camp were killed at his side' (p. 524); Höpfner, 'the loss of the Prussians and Saxons amounted to: 5 officers killed or dead of their wounds, 24 officers wounded, 17—1800 men in dead, wounded and prisoners, 15 Prussian and 18 Saxon guns and the ammunition wagons belonging to them, almost all the troops' baggage, 4 colours' (p. 284); 'the loss of not quite 2000 men was painful for the small forces of the Prussians, but in no way decisive for the outcome of the war'; 'where jäger and fusiliers fought on the extreme left wing, the fight had stayed in balance; the jäger company Valentini had in the action from 10 o'clock in the morning to 4 o'clock in the afternoon only 1 officer and 3 men wounded and 4 men missing' (p. 286); 'General Bevilaqua followed the ... battalion Müffling, but before he could unite with it he was surrounded by the pursuing cavalry, the battalion dispersed, the general himself taken prisoner'; 'General Trützschler was badly wounded, as were Colonel Kaphengst of the Schimmelpfennig [hussars] and Colonel Pflugk of the Saxon hussars'; 'Colonels Rühle and Rabenau taken prisoner'; 'of the magazine in Saalfeld a considerable part, namely of forage, had been saved' (OCR); Mumpfling, 'it was there that the Saxon general Bevilaqua was taken prisoner'; 'General Trutzschlen and Colonel Pfluck, who had distinguished themselves in the combat, were gravely wounded at the same time and the latter was taken prisoner' (OCR); Lannes, as in claim foucart-side-a for the prince's death (p. 464).

claims.value: Saalfeld is a town on the Saxon Saale (Bodart). The gorges leading to Saalfeld are very deep, crossing sheer mountains covered with forests that are mostly impenetrable (the 5th corps's journal, OCR), and General Foucher reported that the division Suchet's park had been caught in the gorges. Prince Louis did not know the ground round Saalfeld at all; he knew only from Captain Valentini that the Coburg road debouched from the mountains there and that at their foot the Saale valley widened more than further down. The outpost officer added that the enemy, apparently strong in cavalry, could act in the ground at Saalfeld, especially on the right flank of the jäger and fusiliers. For lack of room the prince's line deployed by the right, in inversion, so that the Saale lay at its back; Höpfner calls the position not especially advantageous for defence, though the enemy had to debouch from the mountains before its front (OCR). Lannes, reconnoitring, found the ground especially favourable to the French way of fighting: the troops had a commanding position overlooking the whole Saale valley from Saalfeld to Schwarza, while the plain was cut by many small wooded valleys running down to the Saale; trees, bushes, garden walls and earth banks covered the French skirmishers (OCR). Höpfner's first reason for the defeat is the prince's spreading of the 8000 men available over 1 Meile, from Saalfeld to Blankenburg, with the Saale at his back. In M. de Mumpfling's report the prince's troops held a raised ridge commanding the whole valley between Saalfeld and Schwarza while Lannes held villages in low, flat ground; the ground was singularly favourable to French tactics; when the prince led his cavalry in an attack, a French manœuvre and the unevenness of the ground caused disorder and confusion; and the stony, wooded bank of the Saale kept the enemy from pursuing the infantry (OCR).

claims.value: Side A: Lannes reported on the evening of the action that General Foucher did not know where the great artillery park was and needed 500 rounds of 4 and 200,000 infantry cartridges. Foucher reported on 11 October 1806 that the division Suchet's park had been caught in the gorges, so that 2 four-pounders alone fired from the start; that 264 rounds of 4 had been consumed and that the 10 eight-pounders and 2 howitzers that arrived at the end of the action fired 63 rounds in all; and that the infantry had fired 200,000 cartridges, which he asked to have replaced, needing also 4 four-pounder caissons and ammunition for the howitzer of 5 inches 6 lines. In Suchet's report skirmishers who had used up their cartridges were replaced by another regiment, and Foucart's note says that the success of the Elector's regiment's counterattack seems due in part to the exhaustion of a light infantry regiment's skirmishers' ammunition (OCR). On the 11th Lannes could not send the captured guns to Kronach, several being dismounted and not a single horse to be found at Saalfeld; from Neustadt he asked where the great artillery park was, to replace the ammunition the division Suchet had burned the day before (OCR). Side B: the magazine at Saalfeld was being cleared with ox-wagons, which hindered the march through the town; the forage wagons set off from Saalfeld to Rudolstadt, and a considerable part of the magazine, chiefly forage, was saved (OCR). Side B's horse guns, having suffered from the enemy battery and shot off their ammunition, followed the cavalry to replenish it (OCR). The Prussians and Saxons lost 15 Prussian and 18 Saxon guns with their ammunition wagons and almost all the troops' baggage. Höpfner says it soon turned out that guns and wagons could not march from Rudolstadt, Orlamünde or Kahla to Neustadt and Pöllnitz on the steep, bad mountain roads (OCR), and the prince had learned that no usable road led from Rudolstadt to Pösneck, the carriage road going by Saalfeld.

The ammunition and the magazine were means the commanders inherited, but which guns fired, what was used and what was saved followed from their decisions and the timing of the action (claims side-a-command and prince-decision), so the phase is unresolved. The figures are side A's consumption and needs, not its stocks; no return of ammunition on hand was found (open questions). Foucart's note on the counterattack, read in the OCR, is told from M. de Mumpfling's report, which it follows, by its italic type on the page image, viewed for that purpose and not registered. claims.value: Side A's information: on the morning of 10 October 1806 Napoleon wanted to know during the day of the movement on Saalfeld, so that if the enemy had gathered more than 25,000 men there he could send reinforcements by Pösneck and take them in the rear, and the major general wrote to Lannes that nothing led the Emperor to think there could be more than 12 to 15,000 men at Saalfeld. Höpfner's version of Napoleon's order provides for a serious defence of Saalfeld, a concentration of all the enemy's forces there, or an enemy only some 15—18,000 strong, and asks for reports three times a day; until then, he says, Napoleon had no definite knowledge of where his opponent's main forces stood and was groping in the dark (OCR). That morning Napoleon wrote to Marshal Soult that Lannes would reach Saalfeld only that day unless the enemy was there in considerable force, and in the evening that he believed Lannes had attacked Saalfeld that day, that the cannonade had been brisk but short, and that he did not know the result (OCR). Lannes wrote that a brisk fusillade heard that morning toward the centre corps had led him to attack, thinking his movement would make a diversion on the centre. In Suchet's report the skirmishers were met at the debouch by the enemy's fire and the cannon soon announced the enemy's resolution to fight, and in the corps's journal Lannes ordered the advance after convincing himself that the enemy meant to fight (OCR). In Höpfner, Lannes reconnoitred the Prussian position and the ground (OCR); from the height the French overlooked completely the approach of the prince's few battalions and no doubt soon recognised that no significant attack was meant; Höpfner says Lannes could overlook every man in the Prussian position and act under cover with his own forces up to the last decisive moment (OCR). After the action Lannes wrote that the prince's corps appeared to have been made up of 5 regiments, 3 Saxon and 2 Prussian, and 4 regiments of hussars, and the prisoners reported that the King of Prussia was at Erfurt with his army. General Milhaud passed on information gathered at Pösneck that the French had taken Saalfeld and that they had attacked that morning and been repulsed (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 456, 457, 262, 275, 464, 465, 522 and 524) and the OCR as marked. What Lannes knew shaped his decision to attack alone, and what he learned on the field came partly from his own reconnaissance (claim side-a-command), so the phase is unresolved. The major general's estimate of 12 to 15,000 men is above Höpfner's 8300 for the prince's advanced guard and Bodart's 9,000 (claims hoepfner-side-b and bodart-strength). Napoleon's evening letter gives the cannonade's length in hours only in the OCR; the 2nd Bulletin, read from the page image, says it lasted only two hours. English renderings (ours): Napoleon, as in claim side-a-command for the heading, date and the 25,000 (p. 456); the major general, as in claim side-a-command for the heading and date; 'our posts are going to Pösneck and, if the enemy's forces at Saalfeld became too considerable, we would march on them from behind, but nothing leads the Emperor to think that there can be more than 12 to 15,000 men there' (p. 457); Höpfner, as in claim side-a-command for the order (p. 262); 'until then Napoleon still had no definite knowledge of the position of his opponent's main forces, and was groping completely in the dark;' (OCR); Napoleon to Soult, 'the Emperor to Marshal Soult. claims.value: Side B's information: riding from Stadt-Ilm to Rudolstadt the prince received Colonel Rabenau's report that the enemy, 16—20,000 strong, was advancing from Coburg on Gräfenthal and would to all appearance attack Saalfeld seriously the next day, but he doubted that very considerable forces would come by the Saale valley, believing rather that the enemy would direct his main forces by Schleiz against the left flank of the Prussian army. He did not know the ground round Saalfeld at all; from the castle of Rudolstadt the French bivouac fires could be seen. A prisoner said that the column advancing on the Coburg road was Marshal Lannes's advanced guard and that Lannes followed with 30,000 men and had orders to attack, and the outpost officer added that the enemy appeared strong in cavalry. The prince wrote to the Duke of Brunswick that he believed he saw only a strong reconnaissance and could hold the defile of Saalfeld as long as he was attacked only in front, and he thought it possible to tell a mere show from a serious attack (OCR). When the enemy's evident superiority was put to him he made no reply (OCR). By Höpfner's account nobody told him that the crossing of the Saale had been forbidden, and he still believed in Hohenlohe's crossing at the end (OCR). In M. de Mumpfling's report he was no doubt little informed of the strength of the French corps, and later saw that he faced superior forces in a position too extended for his weak corps (the latter OCR).
claims.rationale: Höpfner's account, partly from the page images (pp. 260, 262 and 268) and partly from the OCR; Mumpfling's from the page image (p. 464) and the OCR. The prince's information shaped his decision to advance and fight, and what reached him depended on Hohenlohe's messengers and his own staff (claims prince-decision and side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. Rabenau's 16—20,000 and the prisoner's 30,000 are above Bodart's 12,000 and Höpfner's about 14,000 French engaged (claims bodart-strength and hoepfner-side-a). English renderings (ours): as in claim prince-decision for Rabenau's report and the prince's doubt (p. 260); as in claim saalfeld-ground for the ground (p. 262); 'from the castle of Rudolstadt one could see the bivouac fires of the French' (p. 262); 'a prisoner had been taken. He stated:' (OCR); '[that the] column advancing on the road from Coburg was the advanced guard of Marshal Lannes, who followed with 30,000 men and had the order to attack' (p. 268); as in claim saalfeld-ground for the cavalry (p. 268); 'in the written report to the Duke the prince said that he had advanced to Saalfeld — why he had done this, if the enemy debouched from the mountains — that he believed, however, that he saw only a strong reconnaissance and would be able to hold the important defile of Saalfeld as long as he was attacked only in front, and that it was therefore necessary for the advanced guard of the main army to cover his right flank from Hochdorf'; 'it seemed possible to him to distinguish the mere show from the serious attack, and at least to hold up the enemy until Prince Hohenlohe had crossed the Saale with the ... other columns of his corps,'; as in claim prince-decision for the superiority and the reply; as in claim side-b-command for what the prince was not told; 'it no doubt follows from this that the prince had still believed in the crossing of the Saale by Hohenlohe's corps' (OCR); Mumpfling, as in claims foucart-side-b and prince-decision (p. 464); 'the prince could not be mistaken and noticed that he was dealing with superior forces, and that it was not prudent to continue the fight in a position too extended for his weak corps, unless he counted on prompt' [the sentence continues] (OCR).

claims.value: Side A's objectives: Napoleon wrote on the morning of 10 October 1806 that Lannes would attack Saalfeld 'tomorrow' (claim side-a-command), and the major general told Lannes to hasten Marshal Augereau's arrival and immediately afterwards attack Saalfeld. In Höpfner's version of the order Lannes was to attack an enemy of only some 15—18,000 men together with Augereau, and to seize Saalfeld quickly and post himself there if the Prussians retreated (the last OCR); Höpfner says Napoleon set great weight on holding Saalfeld as the nearest point where the left-wing column could join the other columns, and feared rightly that Lannes, if not careful, might be attacked alone and beaten (OCR). Lannes wrote that he attacked thinking his movement would make a diversion on the centre. On the field, in Höpfner, General Suchet was to debouch with the corps's advanced guard from the valley of Garnsdorf while the corps's cavalry and his division moved along the ridge toward Blankenburg to take from the prince his retreat on Rudolstadt, and the fight in front was to hold the prince before the town while the turning movement took effect (OCR). In M. de Mumpfling's report the French aimed to hold in check the troops on the left above Saalfeld, to cover the whole front of the prince's position with skirmishers, and to edge to the left to envelop the prince and cut him off from the Schwarza (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 456, 457, 262, 464 and 465) and the OCR as marked. The orders set the objective of taking Saalfeld together with Augereau; the diversion, the timing and the turning movement were Lannes's (claim side-a-command), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): as in claim side-a-command for Napoleon's letter, the major general's letter, Höpfner's version of the order and its last clause, Lannes's letter, Suchet's orders and the fight in front; 'Napoleon set great weight on the possession of Saalfeld, as the nearest point of union of the left-wing column with both the other columns, and feared with reason that Marshal Lannes, if he did not go to work cautiously, might be attacked in isolation and beaten' (OCR); Mumpfling, 'the manœuvres of the French army developed more and more: its object was to hold in check the troops posted on the left wing above Saalfeld and to occupy with its skirmishers the whole front of the prince's position, always edging to the left in order to envelop the prince and cut him off from the Schwarza' (OCR).

claims.value: Side B's objectives: Hohenlohe's order was for the prince to defend the posts of Rudolstadt and Blankenburg until the main army's advanced guard arrived and then to withdraw across the Saale toward Pösneck (OCR); in M. de Mumpfling's report, to keep the posts of Blankenburg and Rudolstadt until Lieutenant-General Blücher arrived, hand them over to him and withdraw to Pösneck. By Höpfner's account the prince advanced to Saalfeld because the enemy, if he took it, would bar the advanced guard's crossing of the Saale, cut it off from Hohenlohe's corps and be able to use the bridge and the good road to Neustadt to fall on the corps's flank and reach Neustadt first; because of the magazine there; and to keep the bridge for his own crossing until the main army's troops arrived (partly OCR). Höpfner says that the holding of Saalfeld, to keep the enemy from the nearest road to Neustadt and to keep the crossing for the advanced guard if Hohenlohe gave the definitive order, must be kept in view throughout the prince's arrangements (OCR). At the end the prince resolved on a show of attack to gain time until the main army's troops came near, believing Hohenlohe's crossing still to come, and to drive off the skirmishers who would harass his retreat; it did not occur to him to attack up the heights, but if the enemy halted and made front, all that was wanted was achieved (OCR). He told Captain Valentini that he left Saalfeld unwillingly and wished he could hold on until he had further news from Hohenlohe or the main army's advanced guard came up to take over the post, so that he could cross the Saale to join Tauentzien (OCR). Höpfner holds that the action was lost less through the French superiority than for reasons of which the first is the prince's endeavour to hold both Saalfeld and the retreat on Rudolstadt, two aims he believed he could reach only by spreading the 8000 men available over 1 Meile, from Saalfeld to Blankenburg, with the Saale at his back. In Mumpfling's report the prince resolved to forestall the attack and give battle to save Saalfeld, where there was a magazine.

claims.value: In Lannes's letter, the 2nd Bulletin and Höpfner side A attacked. Lannes wrote that the fusillade heard toward the centre had led him to attack the enemy, and the Bulletin says that he attacked Prince Hohenlohe's advanced guard at Saalfeld on the 10th. In Höpfner the prince took up a position from which he believed he could await the enemy's movements, the enemy having to debouch from the mountains before its front; the French skirmishers, supported by cavalry, drove the jäger posts out of Garnsdorf and seized the debouch, and Lannes had his advanced guard debouch from the valley of Garnsdorf while his cavalry and the division Suchet moved along the ridge to take the prince's retreat (OCR). The prince's last advance, 3½ weak battalions in echelons against the height with the cavalry covering them, was a show of attack to gain time and drive off the skirmishers: it did not occur to him to attack up the heights, and the French, no doubt soon recognising that no significant attack was meant, continued the brigade Wedell's march to the left (partly OCR). When the brigade Wedell had completed its turning movement and attacked General Bevilaqua, the brigade Claparède also went over seriously to the attack (OCR).
claims.rationale: Coded A_attacked: in these accounts Lannes attacked the prince's position, and the prince's advance in Höpfner was a show of attack made from that position to gain time and cover his retreat, which the French recognised as no significant attack; by the brief's rule such a stroke does not make side B an attacker. Lannes decided to attack when he did, on hearing the firing toward the centre and before Augereau came up (claim side-a-command), so the posture is tagged commander_created; Napoleon's orders had provided for an attack on Saalfeld together with Augereau. General Suchet's report and M. de Mumpfling's, coded separately, make the prince's advance a real attack (claim posture-suchet-mumpfling). English renderings (ours): Lannes, as in claim side-a-command (pp. 464 and 465); the Bulletin, as in claim bodart-commanders (pp. 522 and 524); Höpfner, as in claim prince-decision for the position and the show of attack (OCR); 'the enemy advanced with skirmishers supported by troops of cavalry, drove the jäger posts out of Garnsdorf, seized the debouch,' (OCR); as in claim side-a-command for Suchet's orders (OCR); as in claim hoepfner-side-b for the advance, its note and the cavalry and in claim hoepfner-side-a for the French march (p. 275); as in claim side-b-objectives for the heights (OCR); 'by holding those heights the prince believed he would gain not only a point of support for the right wing for the intended show of attack, but also favour the retreat into the Schwarza valley' (OCR); 'now, when the brigade Wedell — ... and ... line infantry regiments — had completed the turning movement by the left and attacked General Bevilaqua and Unter-Wirbach, the brigade Claparède meanwhile also went over seriously to the attack' (OCR).

claims.value: In General Suchet's report and M. de Mumpfling's both sides attacked (OCR, except Mumpfling's opening paragraph). In Suchet's report the French skirmishers were met at the debouch by the enemy's fire and the cannon soon announced his resolution to fight, and in the corps's journal, quoted in it, Lannes, once convinced that the enemy meant to fight, ordered the cavalry and the division Suchet forward; when a French regiment seized the debouch of Beulwitz and pressed the enemy there, the prince, after trying to dislodge it by fire, ordered an infantry charge, and his battalions marched to carry the heights; when Suchet led battalions against their right flank, the Prussian infantry turned about and withdrew into the plain, and Lannes later ordered the charge. In Mumpfling's report the prince resolved to forestall the attack and give battle to save Saalfeld; he had resolved to attack the enemy if it advanced, and once he believed his right flank secured he proceeded to a decisive attack, while the French manoeuvred to hold the troops above Saalfeld in check, cover his whole front with skirmishers and envelop him.
claims.rationale: Coded both_attacked: in these accounts side A attacked the prince's position and the prince made a main attack of his own out of it, a charge to carry the heights (Suchet) or a decisive attack (Mumpfling), not a counterattack inside his position. Mumpfling's decisive attack, made by the regiments Prince Xavier and the Elector formed by battalions in chequer before the right wing, is the advance of the regiments Kurfürst and Xaver in battalion echelons that Höpfner calls a show of attack (claim posture-lannes-hoepfner). Each commander decided at this engagement to attack, Lannes in ordering the advance and the charge and the prince in resolving to attack, so the posture is tagged commander_created. Mumpfling's report is a French translation printed in Foucart's notes. claims.value: No passage read has either side fight from works. Side B stood before the town of Saalfeld, between the town and the Rabenstein with guns on a gentle rise, and in a line deployed with the Saale at its back (on a raised ridge commanding the valley, in M. de Mumpfling's report); side A had to debouch from the mountains before the prince's front and, in Mumpfling's report, held villages in low ground (OCR except the position at the Rabenstein). Two passages name works without showing anyone fighting from them: jäger and fusiliers driven back to the town took the covered way along its ditch and barricaded its gates in haste, while others still held before the town or withdrew fighting; and Höpfner's judgment that the jäger and fusiliers could have held the town, which had a wall and ditch, while the rest crossed the Saale describes a defence that was not made (OCR). Trees, bushes, garden walls and earth banks gave the French skirmishers cover (OCR).
claims.rationale: Code none_named: the places held were the approaches to the town, a ridge, a suburb, villages and mountain slopes, held without named works, and the garden walls covered skirmishers as ground, not as works. The barricaded gates and the town's wall are named, but no passage read has side B fight from them: the gates were barricaded in haste by troops already driven back, and Höpfner names the wall and ditch in his judgment of what the prince could have done. A coding that counted the barricaded gates would give B_fortified, and one that also counted the garden walls that covered the French skirmishers, both_fortified. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim, and a none_named code takes the phase unresolved; none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, as in claim hoepfner-side-b for the position at the Rabenstein (p. 268); as in claim saalfeld-ground for the deployment and the cover and in claim prince-decision for the position (OCR); 'in the long suburb at the gate of the town he already met part of the jäger and fusiliers, who had at last been driven back by the enemy advancing in superior force'; 'they had, leaving the town on the right, taken the covered way along the town ditch, and barricaded the town gates in haste'; 'some troops still held before the town or withdrew fighting'; 'the prince's jäger and fusiliers would have held the town, which had a wall and ditch, against the French advancing from Garnsdorf until the troops had reached their position on the right bank and the Saale bridge had been prepared for destruction or barricading' (OCR); Mumpfling, as in claim saalfeld-ground for the ridge and the villages (OCR).

open_questions: Deferred: M. de Mumpfling's original report, of which Foucart prints a French translation from the war archives in his notes (OCR except the opening paragraph on p. 464); Höpfner's plan of the action, not inspected; Höpfner's footnote on p. 284 naming the officers killed, heavily inked and not transcribed (its OCR is not cited); Saxon accounts and returns, and returns of Lannes's corps, none found in the passages read. In Foucart: the surgeon's report on the prince's wounds, printed as a note to Lannes's letter of 11 October (p. 495, OCR; not cited); General Foucher's three paragraphs on Lieutenant Simonnet and Captain Beaufranchet (p. 497; not transcribed or cited); Lannes's letter of 11 October to the major general beyond its heading and his question about the artillery park (p. 496, OCR); the 2nd Bulletin's figure for the French killed and wounded in all the combats it reports (p. 525, OCR; not cited); and Foucart's comment that the 5th corps marched from Gräfenthal in a single column, using all the roads only to debouch, which differs from Mumpfling's several columns and Höpfner's columns (their number only in the OCR) (p. 467, OCR; not cited; its attribution to Foucart rests on the unregistered page image, viewed only to tell his comments from Mumpfling's text). Figures read only in the OCR are not restated: among them the hours of the day, the strengths in General Milhaud's report, the regiment numbers of the French brigades, the force of Höpfner's alternative crossing at Saalfeld and the squadrons in the prince's last order (p. 278).

Most consequential gap: side A's strength. Bodart gives 12,000 men with 14 guns; Lannes has hardly more than 4,000 men of the division Suchet engaged, the 2nd Bulletin half of that division, and Höpfner about 14,000; the passages read give no return of Lannes's corps. The targeted follow-up searched the parent OCR of Foucart's volume for 'SITUATION' (2 hits: a situation of the artillery park on p. 289 and the situation of the Prussian army on p. 611) and 'Suchet' (30 hits, 15 of them 'division Suchet' once line breaks are collapsed), read each hit in its snippet, read Lannes's letter from Gräfenthal of 9 October on p. 428 (not cited), and read in full and selected the documents of 11 October (pp. 494-497) and the 2nd Bulletin (pp. 522-525). It found no return of the 5th corps, but General Foucher's report gives the French guns that fired, 2 four-pounders from the start and 10 eight-pounders and 2 howitzers at the end, which make Bodart's 14 (our arithmetic), and the Bulletin has half of the division Suchet engaged. A return of the 5th corps for early October 1806 could narrow the gap.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's strength (Bodart 12,000 with 14 guns; Lannes hardly more than 4,000 of the division Suchet engaged; the 2nd Bulletin half of that division; Höpfner about 14,000); side B's strength (Bodart 8 battalions, 7 squadrons and 9,000 men with 42 guns; Höpfner 8300 for the advanced guard, 8000 available and 10 squadrons in the last advance and with the light troops; Foucher 27 pieces firing on the French); the guns taken (Lannes 21 with 6 more expected, then 36 to 40; Foucher 25 guns and 2 howitzers; the Bulletin 30; the parenthesis in Suchet's report, Höpfner and Bodart 33); the prisoners (Lannes about 800; the Bulletin 1,000; the parentheses in Suchet's report 1,500 or 1,800; Bodart 1,100; Höpfner 17—1800 killed, wounded and prisoners together); the dead (the Bulletin 600 left on the field; Bodart 700 killed and wounded); the general taken (Lannes a Prussian general; Höpfner and Mumpfling the Saxon General Bevilaqua); Colonel Pflugk (Höpfner wounded; Mumpfling wounded and taken); the French loss (Suchet 172 for his division; Bodart about 200 with 14 officers); the prince's last advance (Höpfner a show of attack; Suchet a charge to carry the heights; Mumpfling a decisive attack; coded separately); and whether Hohenlohe's order reached the prince (Höpfner: it went to his adjutant, and nobody told him of the forbidden crossing; Mumpfling: the prince received it). Also noted: Napoleon's 'tomorrow' in his letter dated the morning of the 10th, and Bodart's printed 75% for 33 of 42 guns, which is 79% (our arithmetic).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his 14 French guns equal Foucher's 2, 10 and 2, his 33 guns equal Höpfner's 15 and 18 and the parenthesis in Suchet's report, and his 1 general and 28 officers equal Höpfner's 5 killed and 24 wounded, all by our arithmetic; the passages read do not show what he used); Foucart (the French staff edition of 1887, printing the letters of Napoleon, the major general, Lannes, Augereau and Milhaud, Foucher's report, General Suchet's report completed with extracts of the 5th corps's journal, the 2nd Bulletin, and M. de Mumpfling's Saxon report in a French translation from the war archives, with Foucart's own notes; a source line on p. 529, read in a search snippet and not cited, gives the journal as drawn up by General Victor); Höpfner (the Prussian history of 1850, which quotes Clausewitz's posthumous manuscript on the prince's character; second-hand for the French side, and the passages read give no source for Napoleon's order from Nordhalben). Mumpfling's is the only side B account Foucart prints. It is a Saxon witness, not one of the French documents, but it is counted with them in Foucart's family as part of the same edition. No passage read shows dependence between Höpfner and Mumpfling, though both describe the prince's last advance in battalion echelons.
